A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Shallow Alignment research. Their text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across reorganizations.

before.justification: v1 reports original EEG/MEG retrieval experiments, layer-wise evaluations, encoder and projector ablations, and qualitative analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds pooling, fusion, validation-split, channel-selection, subject-consistency and scaling analyses.

M1.justification: v1 uses a single pooled intermediate representation. v2 adds learnable spatial and sample-adaptive pooling, plus multi-layer fusion that independently trains neural encoders and averages their retrieval similarity matrices (Sections 4.7–4.8). These extend the procedure substantially; the original projections and contrastive objective remain.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate THINGS-EEG and THINGS-MEG, with the same participant populations and intra-subject and leave-one-subject-out image-retrieval tasks. The added studies vary splits, channel subsets and model components within this retained coverage.

E2.justification: Tables 1–2 retain the same external comparators: NICE, ATM, Neural-MCRL, UBP and NeuroBridge on EEG, and UBP and NeuroBridge on MEG. The new Figure 4 introduces local pooling comparisons, including center-only averaging and shared spatial weighting alongside adaptive attention heads. The original encoder comparison is retained.

E3.justification: Appendix B.2 adds a 74-concept validation holdout and validation-loss checkpoint selection; B.4 adds seven channel configurations with a stated 30-epoch budget. The reported MEG training set changes from 1,854 to 1,654 concepts, acquisition rate from 1000 to 1200 Hz, and bandpass from 0.1–100 to 0.1–40 Hz. These are documented protocol revisions, without evidence establishing that the retained results were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds pooling and fusion ablations, validation-split robustness, regional/full-channel comparisons, subject-wise optimal-layer analysis, and scaling sensitivity to total versus prefix parameter counts. The original encoder, projector, training-dynamics, UMAP and retrieval-case analyses remain, several relocated to the appendix.

E5.justification: Five independent seeded runs remain specified in both versions, and v1 already reports scaling correlations and significance. v2 adds explicit SEM reporting for pooling and validation comparisons and mean ± standard deviation across ten subjects for the channel analysis. No increase in repeated-run counts is documented.

E6.justification: The numerical results in Tables 1–2 and 4–6 are unchanged. New Figure 4 reports 90.8% Top-1 accuracy for four-layer fusion and 91.3% for fusion with adaptive pooling, compared with the retained 82.6% single-layer configuration. These are additional configurations, not revised same-setting scores. New robustness analyses add further findings, and Section 4.4 corrects ViT-H/14's reported peak depth from 35.5% to 32.3%, matching Table 4.

T1.justification: The mathematical problem formulation, projection and contrastive-loss equations, relative-depth formula and concept-accuracy definition are retained. Neither version supplies theoretical proofs, and v2's additions are procedural or empirical rather than new formal mathematical results.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion shift from a novel alignment strategy that unlocks scaling laws toward a systematic granularity-calibration study that recovers a positive scaling trend. The contributions also add spatial pooling and multi-layer fusion, replacing the earlier emphasis on establishing shared human/model hierarchical granularity.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations linking pooling gains to foreground dilution and attention propagation, and fusion gains to complementary representations with diminishing returns. It also interprets the new channel and subject analyses. Section 4.2 newly identifies the test-split layer sweep as exploratory, materially qualifying how selected-layer results should be interpreted.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-access link, discloses retrospective test-based layer exploration and fixed InternViT L28 use in Tables 1–2, specifies pooling heads and the central patch region, and explains joint-modality UMAP fitting and channel-group construction. Reported hardware changes from RTX 3090 to RTX A6000. These substantially expand reproducibility information beyond the retained architecture and optimizer details.

R1.justification: Sections 2.2–2.3 substantially expand positioning around prior hierarchical brain alignment and representation granularity, including Wen, Seeliger and Tu (2018), Lu (2026), Bau (2017) and Raghu (2021). The revised framing explicitly builds on prior multi-layer/non-final-layer alignment findings, narrowing the earlier novelty positioning; some intrinsic-dimension and noise references are removed.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, several result discussions and conclusion undergo extensive rewriting. Results gain a semantic-focused/implicit/explicit alignment organization. Former Sections 4.7–4.8 move to Appendices B.9 and B.3, while pooling and fusion become main-text sections.

P2.justification: v2 merges v1 Figures 3–5 into a composite Figure 3, relocates the encoder and projector figures, and adds pooling/fusion and four robustness-analysis displays. Figure 1's labels are revised, and the journal template changes title, typography and page layout. The appendix retrieval montages are retained rather than newly added cases.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked the validation, channel-selection and parameter-count controls now supplied in Appendices B.2 and B.4–B.6. These substantially strengthen the central empirical finding, while clearer prior-work attribution, selection disclosures and the narrower scaling-trend claim improve transparency and scientific scope. Pooling/fusion ablations provide useful additional methodological evidence. The validation study addresses checkpoint selection, however, and does not establish independent layer selection; optimal-layer results remain exploratory.
